title: The Story of Who We Are and What We Value
author: Nick Hart
summary: Hart opens by asking whether a school's mission, vision and values would be identifiable at all if the logos were stripped away, and answers that they would not. His diagnosis is structural rather than cosmetic: missions describe the whole education sector, visions pretend the future can be fixed in a sentence, and values amount to moral horoscopes nobody could object to. In their place he borrows Hamel and Prahalad's idea of strategic intent, an ambition too big to be fully planned and too important to ignore, which gives direction without pretending the future is mappable. Crucially, he reinterprets the corporate version for schools, swapping competitive logic for a learning logic aimed at human flourishing and deliberate capacity building. He warns that ambition must be calibrated against a school's fragile resource base and emotional bandwidth, or it alienates the people whose belief sustains it. The second half argues that intent only lives once it is carried by narrative, and offers two devices: a unifying metaphor and a graduate story. A worked example from his own school uses the horizon as metaphor, three intents, and a vivid account of a Year 6 leaver named Aisha whose self-efficacy and agency show up in senior school. The piece closes by reframing leadership as meaning-making rather than alignment.
points: Hart's sharpest test of any mission statement is the cover-the-logo test: if three schools' statements are interchangeable, they describe the sector rather than the school.

Strategic intent is offered as ontologically better suited to complex schools than mission, vision and values because it is a direction rather than a destination, and so tolerates emergence without losing coherence.

The caution that schools have less slack than corporations is well made: overambition in business can be absorbed by investment or mergers, while in a school it simply burns out the staff whose belief gives the intent life.
The graduate story works as a decision-making compass rather than decoration, since it dictates what teachers prioritise, where leaders spend time and what families can expect.

Hart pairs metaphor (emotional coherence, a shared picture people can locate themselves in) with narrative (behaviour-driving feeling), treating story as the delivery mechanism for strategy rather than its packaging.
quotes: The structure sounds elegant on paper but in reality, the three blur and repeat. Schools circle the same territory using slightly different words.

And the values? Reassuringly moral horoscopes. Nobody can challenge the choice of values such as respect, kindness or responsibility. Just as most missions describe the sector, most sets of values describe humanity in general.
Strategic intent is an ambition too significant to be fully planned and too important to be ignored. It gives direction without pretending that the future can be reliably mapped.
Our aim isn’t to defeat the school down the road; it’s to deepen culture, improve teaching and strengthen the human capacity of our communities.

Narrative turns intent into a feeling that drives behaviour. Two tools help leaders do this, metaphor and a graduate story. The opportunity in metaphor is a cohesive idea that captures what the school is becoming.
It is the furthest point that we can see, where the known meets the unknown and no matter how close we get, the horizon keeps moving.
Strategic intent, expressed through story, transforms leadership from a task of alignment to one of meaning-making.
